opus-5.5.text:
Rejection sampling is a really natural baseline, and we looked at it fairly carefully in the s1 work. The idea is simple: if you want the model to "think" for a certain amount of compute, you keep sampling until you get a generation that fits within the budget you want, and then you look at how performance changes as you move that budget around.

What we found was surprising. With rejection sampling we actually saw something like inverse scaling. When we allowed longer generations, accuracy didn't go up the way you'd hope, and in some cases it went down. When you dig into the samples, the reason makes sense. If a reasoning trace ends up being very long, that's often because the model got confused, went down the wrong path, and had to backtrack a lot. The shorter traces that fit within a tight budget tend to be the ones where the model knew what it was doing from the start. So conditioning on length gives you a selection effect, not real "more thinking."

It's also just inefficient. You throw away a lot of samples, and the cost of hitting a specific budget grows quickly as you push toward the tails of the length distribution. So from a control perspective it's not great either.

That's part of why we preferred something like budget forcing, where you directly intervene at decode time. If the model tries to stop early, you suppress the end-of-thinking token and append something like "Wait," which nudges it to keep going and often to double-check its answer. If you want it to stop, you force the end-of-thinking delimiter. That gives you precise control over compute, and you actually see positive scaling: more thinking tokens lead to better accuracy, at least up to a point before it plateaus.

More broadly, I'd frame it as sequential versus parallel scaling. Parallel approaches like majority voting or best-of-N are useful and easy to deploy, and they combine nicely with sequential methods. But I think sequential scaling is more promising, because later computation can build on earlier reasoning: the model can reflect, catch mistakes, and refine. Rejection sampling doesn't really give you that. It just filters what the model would have done anyway.

r001.rationale: It says rejection sampling showed inverse scaling: allowing longer generations did not improve accuracy and sometimes reduced it.

r002.rationale: It explains that very long traces often indicate confusion, wrong turns, and backtracking, while shorter traces tend to start on the right path.

r003.rationale: It describes sampling until a generation fits the budget and discarding many samples, indicating compute control comes from selecting among already-produced generations.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so rejection sampling is one of the simplest ways to spend more compute at test time, and I think its simplicity is both its strength and its limitation. The basic idea is you sample a bunch of candidate responses from the model, and then you have some verifier or reward model or filter that picks the best one. In the simplest case you might just do majority voting, which is kind of a degenerate form of this where the verifier is just agreement across samples.

What we found in our work on s1, and what other people have found too, is that it does scale. If you sample more and you have a decent verifier, accuracy goes up. But the scaling is pretty poor compared to sequential approaches. The curve flattens out fairly quickly, because you're essentially just sampling from the same distribution over and over. If the model has a one percent chance of getting a hard problem right, you need a hundred-plus samples before you even expect to see a correct answer, and then your verifier has to actually pick it out from the ninety-nine wrong ones. So you're bottlenecked twice: once on the base model's coverage, and once on verifier quality.

The thing that I find more interesting is sequential scaling, where the model actually gets to think longer and revise. That's what we did with budget forcing in s1, where you just prevent the model from stopping and append "Wait" so it reconsiders its reasoning. The reason that scales better is that later tokens can condition on earlier ones. The model can catch its own mistake. With rejection sampling, every sample is independent, so there's no mechanism for the model to learn from a failed attempt within the same problem.

That said, I don't want to be too negative about it. Parallel sampling is embarrassingly parallel, so latency is great, and if you have a really strong verifier, like a unit test or a formal checker in math, then rejection sampling is really hard to beat in terms of reliability. It's also a very useful training-time tool. A lot of the reasoning models people are training now use some form of rejection sampling to generate data: sample many, keep the correct ones, fine-tune on those. So it's a bit of a workhorse even if it's not the most elegant way to scale inference.

Where I think things are going is combining the two. You do some sequential reasoning, and then you parallelize over that, and the question becomes how you allocate a fixed compute budget between depth and breadth. My intuition is that sequential should get most of the budget for hard reasoning problems, and parallel is more of a variance reduction on top.

r001.rationale: The response says accuracy rises with more samples but the curve flattens. It does not discuss favoring longer generations or say performance declines as compute increases.

r002.rationale: The response does not describe selecting the longest generations or hypothesize that they tend to follow incorrect reasoning paths.

r003.rationale: It says multiple candidates are sampled before a verifier picks one, but does not identify control over test-time compute as post hoc and available only after those generations are produced.

astra-6.text:
I think rejection sampling is a very simple but powerful way to scale test-time compute. You generate multiple candidate answers, then use some criterion to select one. So instead of asking the model to get it right in a single attempt, you give it more opportunities and spend compute on identifying a good answer.

The key question is how well you can verify those answers. For coding, if you have good tests, you can run the candidates and select one that passes. For more open-ended tasks, judging which answer is best can be almost as difficult as generating it. You might use a reward model, but then you're limited by how reliable that model is.

It's also easy to parallelize, which is attractive for latency. But the candidates don't necessarily learn from each other. If they all make the same mistake, sampling more won't help much. So I see it as a strong baseline, and something that can complement approaches where the model spends more time reasoning or revising an answer.

r001.rationale: The response describes generating multiple candidates and selecting one, but does not say that favoring longer generations leads to declining performance as test-time compute increases.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss selecting the longest generations or suggest that this selection favors reasoning that has gone down incorrect paths.

r003.rationale: The response says candidates are generated first and then one is selected, clearly conveying that rejection sampling controls compute only after multiple generations have been produced.

sol-6.1.text:
I think rejection sampling is a very simple but powerful way to scale test-time compute. You generate multiple candidate answers and then use some kind of verifier to select one. So instead of asking the model to get it right in a single attempt, you give it more opportunities.

The key question is how good your verifier is. For something like code, where you can run tests, you have a fairly concrete signal. For more open-ended tasks, identifying the best answer can itself be difficult. If you can’t reliably distinguish a correct answer from one that just looks convincing, generating more candidates won’t necessarily help.

There’s also a distinction between generating more independent attempts and letting a model spend more time reasoning through one attempt. Rejection sampling gives you the former, and you can parallelize it, which is useful for latency. But it doesn’t necessarily let you solve problems that require a deeper chain of reasoning. I’d view those as complementary ways of spending your compute budget.

r001.rationale: The response does not say that favoring longer generations causes performance to decline as test-time compute increases.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss selecting the longest generations or suggest that they may reflect reasoning down incorrect paths.

r003.rationale: It says candidates are generated before a verifier selects one, but does not identify rejection sampling’s compute control as post hoc or say it is available only after multiple generations have been produced.
